III-B Reference Data Preparation The generative-pipeline development retained the 792-frame training set and 201-frame validation set used in the previous study [ 57 ] . These images covered five Hajj locations: Kaaba/Tawaf, Mina, Arafat, Al-Jamarat, and Safa-Marwah. An additional independent set of 261 real Hajj frames, not included in the training or validation sets, was reserved as generative test set. Source-video IDs were checked to ensure that no source video represented in the 261-frame controlled evaluation set appeared in the training or validation sets. The separate 77-image real test set used for downstream crowd-counting evaluation was not used in the generative-model training, workflow-setting selection, or controlled generation evaluation. To prevent source video overlap, the 261-frame generative evaluation set and the separate 77-image downstream test set were drawn from source videos with IDs distinct from those used in the training and validation data; the 77-image test set was also video-disjoint from the 261-frame generative evaluation set. Further details of the data collection and preprocessing protocol are provided in [ 57 ] . The 792-frame training set was used to fine-tune the LoRA adapters for SD 2.1 and SDXL 1.0, whereas Qwen Image Edit was used without additional fine-tuning. The 201-frame validation set was used to assess and select the model and workflow settings across the three generation pipelines. After these settings were fixed, the same 261 held-out frames served as common reference inputs for the controlled comparison of SD 2.1 + LoRA, SDXL 1.0 + LoRA, and Qwen Image Edit. III-C Candidate Generation Pipelines III-C 1 Diffusion-Based Fine-Tuning Baselines Two diffusion-based baselines were implemented to evaluate whether parameter-efficient adaptation could generate realistic and structurally consistent crowd scenes before adopting the final reference-guided editing workflow. The evaluated baselines were SD 2.1 + LoRA and SDXL 1.0 + LoRA. Both used Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to fine-tune adapter weights on the same 792 real Hajj reference images. The base models were not trained from scratch. This approach reduced training costs and supported adaptation to pilgrimage-site appearance, white-clothed crowds, and illumination variation. To prepare textual conditioning for the diffusion-based baselines, a structured captioning strategy was adopted. First, CLIP-based annotation was used to extract key visual metadata from the image name, including location, time-of-day condition, and crowd-density level. Then, BLIP [ 62 ] was employed to generate an initial image-level caption, which was further enriched with Hajj-specific contextual terms. This strategy combined image-level captions with Hajj-specific contextual information, making it suitable for guiding the Stable Diffusion baselines in generating Hajj crowd scenes with improved contextual consistency. The SD 2.1 + LoRA baseline was selected for the initial prototyping stage because of its lightweight architecture, moderate graphics-memory requirements, and well-established LoRA fine-tuning infrastructure. It used the v21_768ema-pruned.safetensors checkpoint and was fine-tuned at 768 × 768 resolution, which is consistent with the native 768-pixel Stable Diffusion 2.1 checkpoint and supports faster experimentation under moderate hardware constraints. The LoRA adapter used rank 16, LoRA alpha 32, AdamW 8-bit optimization, fp16 mixed precision. The micro-batch size was 1, with gradient accumulation of 4, and an effective batch size of 4. The UNet learning rate was 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} , while the text encoder was kept frozen to preserve the pretrained language representation. Training was conducted for 3 epochs using latent caching, gradient checkpointing. The maximum gradient norm was 1.0, and a warm-up ratio was 0.1. Flip and color augmentations were disabled to avoid unrealistic transformations of sacred-site orientation, Kaaba/Tawaf geometry, and Hajj-specific color appearance. Aspect-ratio bucketing was enabled to support mixed image aspect ratios while training at the target resolution. This baseline was computationally efficient and useful for feasibility testing, but the lower resolution limited fine architectural detail preservation. The SDXL 1.0 + LoRA baseline was included to examine whether higher model capacity and resolution could improve architectural detail, crowd texture, and scene fidelity. It used the sdXL_v10VAEFix.safetensors checkpoint with the SDXL model type flag and the standard LoRA network module. It was fine-tuned under the structured captioning strategy described above. The adapter used LoRA rank 16, LoRA alpha 1, AdamW 8-bit optimization, and bfloat16 mixed precision. The micro-batch size was 1, with gradient accumulation of 4 and an effective batch size of 4. The UNet learning rate was set to 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} , and both SDXL text encoders were trained with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} , allowing the textual conditioning to better associate Hajj-specific caption with visual content. Training was conducted for 8 epochs at 1024 × \times 1024 resolution. Gradient checkpointing was enabled to reduce memory usage, and the multi-resolution noise discount was set to 0.3 to support fine-detail learning. Aspect-ratio bucketing was disabled to enforce square crops and reduce geometric distortion in structured Hajj scenes. III-C 2 Proposed Qwen Image Edit Pipeline The proposed generation pipeline uses Qwen Image Edit as an inference-time, reference-guided image editor within a ComfyUI workflow. In contrast to the diffusion-based LoRA baselines, Qwen Image Edit was not fine-tuned in this study. Instead, 261 real Hajj images were used as structural references, and controlled textual instructions were used to guide the editing process. This design enables targeted modification of selected visual attributes, such as crowd-level condition and illumination, while helping preserve the spatial structure of the original Hajj scene. This property is particularly important for Hajj image, where sacred-site geometry, architectural layout, and crowd organization, people head appearance in the crowd must remain visually consistent for crowd-counting research. The editing instructions are described in Subsection 3.4. Qwen Image Edit was included as a candidate because its reference-guided editing design combines text-based instruction conditioning through Qwen2.5-VL with reference-image conditioning and latent image encoding/decoding through the Qwen Image VAE. Compared with unconstrained text-to-image generation, this design provides several advantages for Hajj crowd-scene synthesis. First, the reference image acts as a structural prior, helping to preserve scene geometry, architectural layout, and location-specific visual elements. Second, editing from real Hajj images supports more plausible crowd appearance and spatial organization. Third, instruction-based editing enables targeted modifications, such as changes in crowd level or illumination, while using the reference image to condition the generation process. Finally, using Qwen Image Edit as an inference-time editor reduces the need for extensive location-specific fine-tuning while supporting controlled synthetic data generation. Based on these advantages, the proposed workflow was implemented in ComfyUI, as shown in Figure 2 . The Qwen Image Edit workflow was implemented using a node-based ComfyUI pipeline. The workflow consists of four main stages, summarized in Table 1 . First, real Hajj reference images are loaded in batches, resized to 1024 × \times 1024, and scaled to a standardized pixel budget. Second, the required pretrained components are initialized, including the Qwen Image Edit diffusion transformer (DiT), Qwen text encoder, and VAE. The workflow uses the svdq-int4_r32-qwen-image-edit-2509-lightningv2.0-4steps.safetensors checkpoint [ 61 ] . No additional fine-tuning of Qwen Image Edit was performed on the Hajj data. Third, positive and negative textual instructions are encoded to guide the desired edits and constrain unwanted changes. The positive instruction specifies the required crowd, illumination, and viewpoint conditions, whereas the negative instruction is used to reduce undesirable artifacts and structural distortions. III-D Instruction Design and Controlled Editing Factors The proposed Qwen Image Edit pipeline relies on structured textual instructions to generate controlled synthetic variations from real Hajj reference images. Unlike open-ended text-to-image prompts, the instructions were formulated as editing commands applied to an existing reference image. Each instruction was designed to modify a specific visual factor while constraining the model to preserve the original scene structure. The main controlled factors were crowd-level condition, illumination/time-of-day condition, reference-view consistency, and location-specific preservation constraints. In this study, crowd-level conditions refer to image-level visual categories, such as very low, low, medium, and high crowd levels. This design was necessary because Hajj scenes contain sacred architectural structures and dense crowd formations, where uncontrolled generation may introduce geometry distortion, unrealistic crowd placement, or inappropriate visual artifacts. The instruction set was developed systematically across five Hajj locations: Kaaba/Masjid al-Haram (Tawaf), Al-Jamarat, Mina, Safa-Marwah, and Arafat. The initial design space contained approximately 240 possible combinations, derived from four crowd-level conditions, four illumination conditions, three reference-view descriptions, and five locations. From this design space, 135 representative instruction templates were selected. The selection criteria included removing redundant prompt variants, prioritizing visually meaningful edits, maintaining architectural diversity across Hajj locations, and refining early trial instructions on the validation set when they produced negligible or unstable visual changes. This process provided representative coverage of the main visual conditions while reducing unnecessary generation cost. Each instruction contains two complementary components. The positive instruction defines the intended edit, such as reducing or increasing visible crowd level, reconstructing exposed ground or floor regions, modifying illumination, or preserving the reference view. The negative instruction listed unwanted changes, including hallucinated buildings, distorted architectural elements, unrealistic body structures, blurred figures, inconsistent shadows, and color shifts in pilgrim clothing. For example, Kaaba/Tawaf instructions emphasize preservation of the Grand Mosque architecture and white marble courtyard; Al-Jamarat instructions preserve bridge geometry and safety railings; Mina instructions emphasize preservation of the tent layout; Safa-Marwah instructions preserve the walkway and rocks; and Arafat instructions preserve natural sand and rock textures. The instruction structure was further adapted to the physical characteristics of each location. Outdoor locations used sun-position and shadow descriptions, such as early morning, midday, golden hour, or evening lighting. Indoor scenes, such as Safa-Marwah, used ceiling-light descriptions instead of sunlight-based illumination. Mina prompts were designed as lighting-only preservation cases, where the tents, crowd layout, and reference viewpoint were kept unchanged while illumination conditions were varied.
